name: Machine Matrix
topics_techniques_covered: figural_matrix: 2x2 and 3x3 matrix completion (missing bottom-right cell)
figural_matrix: Raven-like relational rules running across rows and columns
figural_matrix: abstract colored shapes varying by shape/color/size/position
figural_matrix: RPM rule taxonomy - constant-in-a-row, progression, distribution-of-three, arithmetic add/subtract of a numeric attribute
figural_matrix: logical relations (XOR, OR, AND, consistent union) over attributes (size, color, position, number)
figural_matrix: cognitive-model-driven difficulty (rule count x abstraction x perceptual load)
one_liner: The child taps the one tile that completes a glowing figural matrix so the machine powers on.
interaction: A 2x2 or 3x3 grid is shown with the bottom-right cell empty and 4-6 candidate tiles in a tray below. The child taps a candidate to snap it into the empty cell (tapping another candidate swaps it), then taps the pulsing GO button to submit. One confirmed selection is the answer; no typing, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand hovers the empty cell, glides to the correct tray tile, taps it (it snaps into the cell), and the machine lights up - under 10s. Then one unscored 2x2 warm-up gives a green pulse for correct or a gentle shake plus the answer for wrong, before scored items begin.

learning_science.principle: Cognitive load theory - minimize extraneous load
learning_science.why: Written rubrics and notation add extraneous load that masks the reasoning being measured.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Zero text; a wordless ghost-hand demo and snap-to-cell tiles carry all instruction so working memory is spent on the relations, not the interface.
learning_science.source: Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas (1998), Educational Psychology Review 10(3)

learning_science.why: Reasoning difficulty is set by how many relations must be bound simultaneously, the true tail driver in matrices.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty escalates by adding co-acting rules (1 to 4) rather than surface clutter, so the ceiling probes relational binding capacity.
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6)

learning_science.principle: Process account of the Raven Progressive Matrices
learning_science.why: RPM ability is explained by rule induction and goal management over a fixed rule taxonomy.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items are generated from the constant/progression/distribution-of-three/arithmetic rule set with distractors keyed to specific rule violations.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990), Psychological Review 97(3)

learning_science.why: A demonstrated solution before independent practice lowers load and speeds schema formation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The ghost-hand solves one item fully (worked example); the warm-up fades to a hint-only glow; scored items are unguided.
learning_science.source: Renkl & Atkinson (2003), Educational Psychologist 38(1)

new_measurements_proposed.name: Rule dimensionality solved
new_measurements_proposed.what: Number of independent relational rules or attributes the child integrated simultaneously in the correct answer (e.g., a 3x3 matrix solved under three co-acting rules).
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Separates children by the relational complexity they can bind at once (Halford). Two children may both be correct, but at 1 vs 3 co-acting rules; exposing that structure sharpens tail placement where a single difficulty index blurs it, and it is harder to coach than surface speed.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Tag each item with its rule set and design distractors so each foil violates exactly one named rule; the chosen option reveals which rule-dimensions were satisfied. Log the maximum simultaneously satisfied rules on correct high-complexity items.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=6 items whose distractors are orthogonally keyed to individual rules, spanning 1 to 4 co-acting rules near the child's edge.

tail_precision_rationale: M-DIFFREACH under adaptive rule-count escalation is the single sharpest tail statistic - it walks each child to the exact number of co-acting rules they can bind before failing. M-ERRTYPE reads the chosen distractor against a per-rule violation key, so a near-miss (correct on 2 of 3 rules) marks latent ability just below the cut and separates it from random error. M-RTFIRST captures reflective encoding (able solvers look longer before the first tap) and M-REV distinguishes confident single placements from guess-and-check, turning one hard matrix into a rule-resolved ability estimate rather than a single right/wrong bit.
age_rationale: K-1 gets 2x2 single-rule items with large tap tiles and snap-to-cell placement (no fine drag, no reading), matching limited fine-motor precision and pre-literacy. 2-3 adds a second rule and 3x3 grids; 4-5 and 6-8 add abstraction, arithmetic/logical rules, and perceptually confusable distractors. The same shell spans all bands purely by rule count and abstraction.

adaptive.content_range: single-rule 2x2 figural completion (K-1) up to 3-4 co-acting-rule 3x3 abstract matrices with arithmetic/logical relations (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: rule type constant to progression to distribution-of-three to arithmetic to XOR/AND/OR
attribute count and type (shape, color, size, number, position, rotation)
adaptive.notes: Fully procedurally generable from a rule x attribute grammar with distractors keyed to individual rule violations; supports a bottomless above-level bank for ceiling probing and parallel clones for consistency checks.

engagement_hook: Powering up a machine - the correct tile makes gears spin and lights cascade for an immediate juicy success cue, and escalating rule complexity feels like unlocking harder levels.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Guard perceptual load (keep distractor similarity a deliberate lever, not accidental noise); avoid color-only rules by pairing color with shape/pattern for color-vision differences; big snap-to-cell tiles remove motor-precision demands; ghost-hand plus warm-up neutralizes game-novelty variance; do not over-reward speed since reflective latency is expected on hard items.

name: What Comes Next
topics_techniques_covered: figure_series: a sequence changes by a consistent rule across the row; pick the figure that continues it (NNAT serial-reasoning format)
figure_series: incomplete progressive sequence; choose the option that best continues the series (CFIT format)
figure_series: row progression on one or more attributes (size up, fixed-step rotation, increasing count)
figure_series: simple repeating or growing picture pattern (AB AB, or +1 dot each step)
one_liner: The child taps which figure comes next to continue a left-to-right pattern.
interaction: A row of 3-5 figures ends in a question slot with 4 options in a tray below. The child taps the option that continues the sequence; it snaps into the slot (tap another to swap), then taps GO to submit. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sweeps left-to-right along the row with a rhythmic pulse on each figure (implying and then...), then taps the option that fits the slot; the row completes and glows. One AB-AB warm-up trial runs before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Motion plus static form can convey sequence and change without any words.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The demo animates the left-to-right sweep so temporal ordering is shown rather than told, staying on the visual-only channel.
learning_science.source: Mayer (2009), Multimedia Learning (2nd ed.), Cambridge University Press

learning_science.principle: Fluid intelligence via inductive rule extraction
learning_science.why: Serial reasoning taps culture-fair Gf by requiring rule induction from a figural progression.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Sequences are built from attribute progressions (size, count, rotation) so the task loads inductive reasoning rather than crystallized knowledge or notation.
learning_science.source: Cattell (1963), Journal of Educational Psychology 54(1)

learning_science.why: Matched clones at the same difficulty reduce the conditional standard error of a tail decision.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each scored item ships with an AIG-cloned twin at the same rule set so response consistency can be logged.
learning_science.source: Embretson & Reise (2000), Item Response Theory for Psychologists

tail_precision_rationale: The scored pair are AIG twins (same rule set, new surface), so M-CONSIST flags inconsistent near-cut responders for extra items and shrinks the conditional standard error exactly where decisions are hardest. M-ERRTYPE separates a periodicity slip (picking the previous term) or an off-by-one step (near-miss) from a random pick, refining where below the cut a child sits. M-RTFIRST with M-RT credit reflective extraction of a multi-attribute rule over fast single-attribute pattern-matching.
age_rationale: K-1 sees short repeating patterns (AB AB, +1 dot) with big tap targets and no reading. 2-3 adds single-attribute progressions; 4-5 combines two attributes; 6-8 uses fixed-step rotation plus count/size progressions with closer distractors. Continuation is developmentally accessible early, so the shell spans all four bands.

adaptive.content_range: AB-AB and +1 growing patterns (K-1) up to multi-attribute progressions with fixed-step rotation and count (6-8)
difficulty_levers: pattern type repeat to single progression to multi-attribute progression
step size and whether step is constant or accelerating
distractor closeness: off-by-one step, previous term, wrong attribute
adaptive.notes: A sequence grammar generates unlimited parallel forms; twin clones at equal difficulty enable consistency and drift checks.

engagement_hook: A marching parade of shapes that begs to be completed; snapping the right next figure triggers a satisfying continue-the-beat animation.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Avoid reading and numeral knowledge (use dots/shapes, not written numbers, for count); large tap options remove motor demands; key distractors to specific rule errors to block surface guessing; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; keep pacing self-directed so processing speed does not contaminate the reasoning score.

name: Odd One Out
topics_techniques_covered: odd_one_out: five figures shown; select the one that does not belong (CFIT classification format)
odd_one_out: several figures share a generated rule except one; pick the figure that breaks the rule
odd_one_out: four pictures where three share an obvious property and one does not
odd_one_out: four shapes where three follow a simple rule (all have three sides) and one does not
one_liner: The child taps the single figure that does not belong with the others.
interaction: Four to six figures appear in a row or grid. The child taps the one that breaks the shared rule; the tapped figure lifts and highlights (tap another to change the choice), then taps GO to confirm. One decisive selection is the answer; no typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand scans across the figures pausing with a small nod on each that belongs, then taps firmly on the different one, which pops out of line. A warm-up (three triangles and one circle) runs unscored first.

learning_science.why: Discriminating among close alternatives forces deeper feature analysis than spotting a lone target.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Older bands use distractors that share all but one attribute, so the child must test each candidate feature - a productive difficulty rather than clutter.
learning_science.source: Bjork & Bjork (2011), in Psychology and the Real World

learning_science.why: The slowest, not fastest, responses index ability, so consistency across trials matters more than peak speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The type runs several quick trials and logs RT variability and the slowest responses rather than crediting raw speed.
learning_science.source: Coyle (2003), Intelligence 31(6)

learning_science.why: Starting from an obvious contrast builds the schema before harder discriminations.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The first scored item uses a salient single-feature odd-one; the next raises shared-attribute overlap.
learning_science.source: Sweller (1988), Cognitive Science 12(2)

tail_precision_rationale: Several fast classification trials yield M-RTVAR and M-LAPSE, whose low variability and few slow lapses track ability better than peak speed (worst-performance rule) and resist coaching. M-ERRTYPE tags which shared attribute a wrong tap honored, distinguishing a defensible alternative grouping (near-miss, latent ability) from a random or salience-driven error. Because trials are short and cloneable, the type contributes many stable RT samples that firm up the tail estimate without fatigue.
age_rationale: K-1 sees four items with one obvious single-feature outlier and big tap targets. 2-3 through 6-8 raise the item count and the attribute overlap of distractors so the odd-one requires multi-feature analysis. Single-tap response and no reading keep it accessible to the youngest band.

adaptive.content_range: one obvious single-feature outlier among four (K-1) up to a subtle multi-attribute generated rule among six (6-8)
difficulty_levers: number of shared attributes among the belongers
adaptive.notes: Generated by sampling a rule for the set then perturbing one figure; unlimited clones and easy difficulty titration; short trials give many RT samples.

engagement_hook: Spot-the-stranger snap judgment with a satisfying pop when the outlier is ejected; quick rounds create a light game rhythm.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Ensure exactly one defensible answer (audit for alternative valid groupings) so near-miss coding is meaningful; do not reward mere speed; pair color with shape so color-vision differences do not create false outliers; a single large tap target removes motor load; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Join the Club
topics_techniques_covered: figure_classification: three figures share a hidden property; pick the figure that belongs with the set
figure_classification: four figures share one generated attribute value; pick the fifth that also fits
figure_classification: three pictures belong together (e.g. things that fly); pick the fourth that belongs
figure_classification: pick the figure that shares BOTH generated attributes (shape count AND fill)
nonverbal_deduction: choose the figure where a spatial condition holds (dot inside the circle but outside the square; star above the box AND inside the ring)
one_liner: Three figures already belong to a club; the child taps the option that also belongs.
interaction: A framed club shows 3 figures sharing a hidden property; 4 candidate figures sit below. The child taps the candidate that belongs (shares the property); it slides into the club frame (tap another to swap), then taps GO to submit.
self_teach: The ghost-hand circles the 3 club members (gesturing they go together), then picks the matching candidate and drops it into the frame, which glows to accept. Warm-up: a club of three red things, pick the red one.

learning_science.why: Classification is inducing the concept that unifies exemplars, a core fluid-reasoning process.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The club shows positive exemplars only; the child must induce the shared concept and test candidates against it, mirroring concept-attainment.
learning_science.source: Bruner, Goodnow & Austin (1956), A Study of Thinking

learning_science.why: Belonging can rest on relational or conjunctive properties, not just surface features.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Higher bands require sharing BOTH attributes or a spatial relation (above AND inside), pushing from surface to relational matching.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), Cognitive Science 7(2)

learning_science.why: Starting concrete then moving abstract supports transfer of the classification schema.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses familiar picture categories (things that fly); older bands fade to abstract shape attributes.
learning_science.source: Fyfe, McNeil, Son & Goldstone (2014), Educational Psychology Review 26(1)

tail_precision_rationale: M-EXPLORE logs how many candidates the child inspects (hovers or tentative taps) before committing; systematic checking of each option against the induced rule marks a strategic tail solver versus a first-glance guesser. M-ERRTYPE identifies which single attribute a wrong choice matched, so a one-attribute match on a two-attribute item is a graded near-miss that places the child just below the conjunctive-reasoning cut. M-RTFIRST indexes rule-induction time before acting, and pairing it with M-RT credits reflective over impulsive responding.
age_rationale: K-1 uses concrete single-attribute categories with big tap targets and no reading. 2-3 moves to abstract single attributes; 4-5 and 6-8 require conjunctive (both-attribute) or spatial-relation membership. Selection-by-tap and positive-only exemplars keep the youngest band supported.

adaptive.content_range: concrete single-attribute category membership (K-1) up to dual-attribute or spatial-conjunction membership with confusable distractors (6-8)
difficulty_levers: single attribute to conjunction of two attributes to spatial relation
distractor overlap with the club rule
adaptive.notes: Club rule and distractors are procedurally sampled; spatial-condition variants generate deduction items sharing the same shell.

engagement_hook: Getting into an exclusive club - the frame glows and welcomes the right newcomer, a belonging hook that makes finding the rule feel worthwhile.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Use positive exemplars that uniquely determine one rule (avoid ambiguous clubs); pair color with shape/pattern; keep picture categories culturally common for the youngest band; large tap targets remove motor load; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; audit conjunctive items so only the keyed option satisfies both attributes.

name: Fill the Grid
topics_techniques_covered: nonverbal_deduction: a partly-filled grid must contain each shape once per row and column; deduce which shape must occupy the target cell
nonverbal_deduction: a 2x2 grid where each row and column shows each of two shapes once; place the shape forced into the empty cell
nonverbal_deduction: a 3x3 shape grid where each shape appears once per row and column; deduce the shape forced into the target cell (child Latin-square version)
one_liner: The child fills the empty cell(s) so each symbol appears exactly once in every row and column.
interaction: A 2x2 or 3x3 grid is partly filled with symbols and has one or more empty cells, with a symbol palette beside it. The child taps a palette symbol then taps an empty cell to place it (or taps a filled cell to clear), snapping to the grid; when all empties are filled the child taps GO. Large snap cells; no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand points along the row then down the column of an empty cell (a highlight sweep), revealing which symbol is missing, then drops it in; the grid glows solved. Warm-up: a 2x2 with two symbols and one empty cell.

learning_science.why: Latin-square cells are fixed by intersecting row and column constraints, exercising deduction rather than pattern guessing.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items are generated so the target cell is logically forced, and the path of deductions can be scored.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990), Psychological Review 97(3)

learning_science.why: Showing the row-and-column check once offloads the strategy so the child can deploy it independently.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The ghost-hand demonstrates the intersect-and-eliminate check; the warm-up fades to a self-run check.
learning_science.source: Sweller & Cooper (1985), Cognition and Instruction 2(1)

learning_science.why: A multi-cell grid yields graded evidence from a single rich item.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Multi-empty grids are scored by cells-correct so one item behaves like several dichotomous ones.
learning_science.source: Embretson & Reise (2000), Item Response Theory for Psychologists

tail_precision_rationale: M-PATH records the order of placements, revealing whether the child fills the most-constrained cell first (forward deduction) or guesses and backtracks; economical, correctly ordered solving at 3x3 is a clean tail separator. M-EFF compares placements and undos to the minimal deduction sequence and M-REV counts backtracks, so children who deduce rather than trial-and-error stand out even at equal accuracy. M-POLY extracts graded ability from one multi-cell grid, sharpening theta with fewer items at the cut.
age_rationale: K-1 gets a 2x2 with two symbols and a single forced empty cell, using big tap-to-place targets and no reading. 2-3 uses a fuller 2x2 or easy 3x3; 4-5 and 6-8 use 3x3 and up with more symbols, fewer givens, and multiple empties requiring chained deduction. Tap-place-clear interaction removes fine-drag demands for the youngest.

adaptive.content_range: 2x2 two-symbol single-forced-cell (K-1) up to 3x3-plus multi-empty chained deduction with sparse givens (6-8)
difficulty_levers: number of empty target cells (single vs chained)
whether a naked-single suffices or an elimination chain is required
adaptive.notes: Latin squares are generated then cells removed to a target deduction depth with a guaranteed unique solution; unlimited clones and precise difficulty control.

engagement_hook: A mini logic-puzzle (sudoku-lite) with a satisfying click as each forced symbol locks in and the grid completes with a glow.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Guarantee a unique forced solution so path and efficiency scoring are valid; use distinct shapes plus color (not color alone); tap-to-place with clear-on-tap avoids fine-drag precision; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; keep symbol count low for young bands so working memory does not confound deduction.

name: Shape Morph
topics_techniques_covered: figure_analogy: A is to B as C is to ? using geometric shapes; infer the A-to-B transformation and apply it to C (NNAT format)
figure_analogy: two figures related by a rule, then a third with options; pick the figure completing the analogy (ICAR figural analogies)
figure_analogy: simple A:B::C:? with one clear change (e.g. big to small)
figure_analogy: A:B::C:? with two shapes changing by one combined rule (size and shade)
one_liner: A first shape turns into a second; the child makes the third shape change the same way by picking the matching fourth.
interaction: The top row shows A with an animated morph arrow into B. The bottom row shows C, an arrow, and an empty slot with 4 options below. The child taps the option that is to C what B is to A; it snaps into the slot. An optional two-icon confidence tap (a star for sure, a wavy hand for not sure) appears, then GO submits.
self_teach: The ghost-hand replays the A-to-B morph (e.g., big shrinks to small), then applies the same shrink to C and taps the matching option; the analogy row lights up. Warm-up: big circle to small circle, so big square to ? (small square).

learning_science.why: Analogical reasoning requires mapping the relation, not the surface, from base to target.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractors include a literal copy of C and a wrong-transform foil so only relational mapping, not surface matching, is credited.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), Cognitive Science 7(2)

learning_science.why: Children move from surface to relational responding as knowledge and working memory grow, setting a floor age for abstract figural analogy.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Bands start at grades 2-3 with a single obvious change and add a second combined rule by 6-8, matching the relational shift.
learning_science.source: Rattermann & Gentner (1998), in Piaget, Evolution, and Development

learning_science.why: Confidence accuracy adds incremental validity and down-weights lucky guesses at the tail.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A quick optional two-level confidence tap is collected on a subset so calibration can be modeled without burden.
learning_science.source: Fleming & Lau (2014), Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 8:443

tail_precision_rationale: M-ERRTYPE uses a designed distractor set - a literal-copy foil (no transform applied), a wrong-attribute foil, and an over/under-application foil - so a wrong answer reveals exactly where the relational mapping broke and grades how far below the analogy cut a child sits. On two-rule items the same distractor keying feeds the proposed M-RULEID (how many transformations were correctly applied), separating one-rule from two-rule mappers at the tail. M-RTFIRST captures the map-before-act latency typical of strong reasoners, and M-CONF on a subset removes lucky guesses via confidence-accuracy calibration.
age_rationale: Figural analogy requires holding an abstract transformation and re-applying it. With familiar relations this appears early, but reliable mapping over arbitrary figural transforms is not dependable until roughly grades 2-3 (ages 7-9); K-1 is excluded because at ages 5-6 such mapping is unstable and would measure developmental stage rather than reasoning (Goswami 1992; Rattermann & Gentner 1998). 2-3 uses one salient change; 4-5 a clear single transform with confusable foils; 6-8 combines two transforms. Big tap options keep motor demands low.

adaptive.content_range: single obvious transform A:B::C:? (grades 2-3) up to two combined transforms with relational distractors (6-8)
difficulty_levers: transformation type: size, rotation, fill/shade, count, reflection, add/delete element
distractor design: literal-copy, wrong-attribute, over-application foils
adaptive.notes: A:B::C:? items generate from a transform grammar with relationally-keyed distractors; unlimited clones and clean difficulty control via transform count.

engagement_hook: A magic morph - watching A visibly transform into B and then casting the same spell on C is playful and makes the hidden rule tangible.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Exclude K-1 to avoid measuring the relational shift instead of reasoning; include a literal-copy foil so surface matching does not score; pair shade/color with shape; keep the confidence tap optional and non-punitive; big tap options remove motor load; the ghost-hand morph plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Sorting Gate
topics_techniques_covered: visual_rule_discovery: two sets of six figures; the left satisfy a hidden rule and the right violate it - discover the rule that distinguishes the sets
visual_rule_discovery: two labeled bins each show a few example figures; place new figures into the bin whose secret rule they match
one_liner: Two bins each show example figures; the child drops each new figure into the bin whose secret rule it matches.
interaction: Two bins (shown by icon, not words) each display 3-4 example figures obeying a hidden rule (e.g., left = has a hole, right = solid). New figures appear one at a time; the child drags each into a bin (or taps the figure then taps a bin) and gets an immediate settle/glow. After a fixed number of figures the child taps GO to score the final placements. A hint lamp can be tapped to reveal one extra worked example.
self_teach: The ghost-hand picks the first queued figure, hovers it over the left bin then the right bin (weighing it), then drops it into the correct bin, which accepts with a glow while the wrong bin gives a soft nudge back. Warm-up uses an obvious color rule (red bin, blue bin).

learning_science.principle: Concept attainment / rule discovery by hypothesis testing
learning_science.why: Inducing a category boundary from positive and negative examples is prototypical inductive reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child must infer the hidden rule from exemplars and test it by placement, with feedback enabling hypothesis revision.
learning_science.source: Bruner, Goodnow & Austin (1956), A Study of Thinking

learning_science.principle: Feedback that informs the next action
learning_science.why: Immediate task-level feedback drives the fastest correct rule revision.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each placement gives instant accept/nudge feedback so the child can update the hypothesis on the very next figure.
learning_science.source: Hattie & Timperley (2007), Review of Educational Research 77(1)

learning_science.why: Gameplay actions can be logged as evidence of competency without stopping to test.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The placement stream is logged as evidence of rule induction (accuracy trajectory, test informativeness), not only a final score.
learning_science.source: Shute (2011), in Computer Games and Instruction

new_measurements_proposed.name: Hypothesis-search efficiency
new_measurements_proposed.what: Informativeness of the child's exploratory choices during rule discovery: how quickly errors are eliminated and whether placements test maximally disambiguating cases versus redundant or random ones.
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: In rule-discovery tasks, able children run efficient disambiguating tests and converge fast; this indexes inductive/scientific reasoning and dynamic-assessment learning rate, adding tail signal beyond final accuracy and resisting coaching.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: From the placement/action log, compute the reduction in the viable-rule space per action (or trials-to-criterion after the first informative feedback) and flag perseverative or random tests.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=1 rule-discovery item with >=6 feedback-bearing actions; aggregate over >=3 such items for a stable rate.

tail_precision_rationale: M-PROG turns one puzzle into a rule-acquisition curve: running accuracy across placements shows how fast the child locks the hidden rule (trials-to-criterion), a dynamic-assessment learning-rate signal with tail validity beyond a static score. The proposed M-HYP scores how disambiguating each placement is (does the child test the informative ambiguous cases or only obvious ones), isolating strategic inductive reasoners at the ceiling. M-HINT (hint-free discovery is stronger evidence) and M-EXPLORE round out a process picture a single accuracy bit cannot give.
age_rationale: Rule discovery from examples requires generating and revising hypotheses, which is unreliable in K-1; the youngest band is served by the five simpler FLU types instead. 2-3 uses a single-feature hidden rule with feedback; 4-5 uses less salient single features; 6-8 uses conjunctive or relational hidden rules with no feedback until GO. Drag or tap-to-bin with large targets keeps motor demands modest.

adaptive.content_range: single obvious-feature sort with feedback (grades 2-3) up to conjunctive/relational hidden rules with delayed feedback (6-8)
difficulty_levers: rule complexity: single feature to conjunction to relational/relational-count
number of worked examples before testing
feedback immediate vs delayed to GO
adaptive.notes: Rules and exemplar sets are procedurally sampled but require an audit that the exemplars uniquely identify the intended rule, so cloning is high-throughput with a uniqueness check.

engagement_hook: Cracking a secret sorting rule - each correct drop confirms your theory with a glow, and the aha of guessing the rule is intrinsically rewarding.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Audit that exemplars determine a unique rule so M-HYP and M-PROG are meaningful; pair color with shape/pattern; large bins and snap placement reduce motor load; keep hints non-punitive but logged; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; exclude K-1 to avoid floor effects that would misread as low ability.

name: Copy the Change
topics_techniques_covered: visual_rule_discovery: a few input-to-output grid examples demonstrate a transformation rule; infer the rule and construct the output grid for a new input
visual_rule_discovery: one worked example shows a small grid changing (e.g. all shapes shift right); apply the same change to a new grid by tapping cells
one_liner: A small example shows a grid changing; the child makes the same change happen on a new grid by tapping cells.
interaction: The top shows a worked example as an animated before-to-after grid pair. Below sit a new before grid and an editable after grid (initialized as a copy of the new before). The child taps cells to change them (a tap cycles a cell through the available colors/states; tap-and-hold clears) to produce the transformed output, then taps GO. Snap-to-cell tapping; no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand plays the example transform (e.g., every filled cell slides one column right) as an animation, then on the new grid taps the cells to reproduce the same slide; the output glows when it matches. Warm-up: a one-row 1x3 shift.

learning_science.principle: Abstraction and reasoning from few examples
learning_science.why: Inferring a transformation from one or few input-output pairs and applying it to a new case is a hallmark of fluid intelligence.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items give one or few worked transforms and require constructing (not selecting) the output, following the ARC abstraction-and-reasoning paradigm.
learning_science.source: Chollet (2019), On the Measure of Intelligence, arXiv:1911.01547

learning_science.why: A studied example plus a completion problem builds a transferable schema at lower load than open problem solving.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child studies the animated example, then completes the analogous output - a completion-problem design.
learning_science.source: Renkl & Atkinson (2003), Educational Psychologist 38(1)

learning_science.why: Building an output rather than picking one yields per-cell graded evidence and blocks lucky guessing.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The output is scored per cell (polytomous) so near-correct constructions earn graded credit.
learning_science.source: Embretson & Reise (2000), Item Response Theory for Psychologists

tail_precision_rationale: Because the child constructs the output, M-POLY scores per-cell correctness so a near-correct grid (right rule, one slip) earns graded credit and places the child precisely where free selection cannot. M-PATH with M-EFF compare the child's edit sequence to the minimal set of changes: constructing exactly the needed cells (no flailing) at a multi-rule transform is a strong ceiling separator and feeds the proposed M-HYP for how systematically the rule was applied. M-REV and M-PROG show whether the child locked the rule immediately or converged by trial-and-error. Guessing is near-impossible for a constructed grid, so accuracy at high difficulty is unusually clean tail evidence.
age_rationale: Constructing a transformed grid demands inferring a rule and executing multiple coordinated edits, exceeding K-1 fine-motor control and working memory; K-1 is covered by the simpler selection-based FLU types. 2-3 applies a single shown transform (shift/recolor) on a small grid; 4-5 infers the transform from one example; 6-8 infers multi-step or conditional transforms on larger grids. Tap-to-cycle cells with large targets keep edits feasible from grade 2 up.

adaptive.content_range: apply a single shown transform on a small grid (grades 2-3) up to infer-and-construct multi-step or conditional transforms on larger grids (6-8, ARC-like tail)
difficulty_levers: transformation complexity: translate to recolor to reflect/rotate to conditional/relational
grid size and number of objects
one worked example vs infer from multiple examples
whether the examples imply a single vs multiple plausible rules
adaptive.notes: Transforms are program-sampled and applied to random grids to make input-output pairs; needs a check that the shown examples imply a unique transform, so cloning is high-throughput with a uniqueness audit.

engagement_hook: You are the copy-machine wizard - learn a secret change from one example then perform it yourself; building the answer feels like casting the rule rather than picking from a menu.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Ensure the example(s) imply a unique transform so per-cell scoring is fair; large tap-to-cycle cells plus undo reduce motor and slip errors; pair color with pattern; no reading; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; exclude K-1 due to multi-edit motor and working-memory demands.

name: Build the Tile
topics_techniques_covered: figural_matrix: 3x3 matrix completion where the missing tile is CONSTRUCTED rather than selected from options
figural_matrix: Raven-like relational rules running across rows and columns
figural_matrix: abstract colored shapes varying by shape/color/size/position
figural_matrix: RPM rule taxonomy - constant-in-a-row, progression, distribution-of-three, arithmetic add/subtract of a numeric attribute
figural_matrix: cognitive-model-driven difficulty (rule count x abstraction x perceptual load)
matrix_induction: derive each attribute of the missing cell from co-acting row/column rules
one_liner: Instead of picking a tile, the child BUILDS the missing matrix cell by setting its shape, color and number so every row and column rule holds.
interaction: A 2x2 or 3x3 matrix shows the bottom-right cell empty. Below sit attribute pickers: a row of shape buttons, a row of color swatches, and a count stepper (1-3 dots). Tapping a picker updates a live preview tile that appears in the empty cell. The child sets each attribute (any order, can change freely) then taps GO to submit the constructed tile. No option tray, no typing, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand sweeps a row then a column of the empty cell (showing where the rules meet), taps the correct shape, the correct color, then the correct count; the preview tile assembles live and the matrix glows. One unscored single-attribute 2x2 warm-up (set only the shape) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Producing an answer rather than recognizing one yields deeper encoding and blocks recognition-only guessing, so the score reflects genuine rule derivation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child constructs the tile attribute-by-attribute instead of choosing among ready-made options, so each attribute must be independently derived.
learning_science.source: Slamecka & Graf (1978), Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory 4(6)

learning_science.why: Matrix difficulty is set by how many relations must be bound at once, the true tail driver.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each attribute (shape, color, count) carries its own row/column rule, so the number of co-acting rules the child resolves is read directly from which attributes are correct.
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6)

learning_science.principle: Process account of the Raven Progressive Matrices
learning_science.why: RPM ability is rule induction plus goal management over a fixed rule taxonomy.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Attributes are governed by the constant/progression/distribution-of-three/arithmetic rule set so construction taps the same induction RPM measures.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990), Psychological Review 97(3)

learning_science.why: A constructed multi-attribute answer yields graded evidence from one rich item.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scoring is per-attribute-correct (0..k) so a tile right on 2 of 3 attributes earns graded credit and behaves like several dichotomous items.
learning_science.source: Embretson & Reise (2000), Item Response Theory for Psychologists

tail_precision_rationale: Because the tile is CONSTRUCTED, M-POLY reads exactly which of the co-acting attribute-rules the child satisfied, and M-RULEID reports the maximum simultaneously-satisfied rules - a per-child relational-complexity ceiling that a single right/wrong bit cannot expose. M-ERRTYPE names the specific attribute-rule missed (a color-progression slip vs a count-arithmetic slip), so a near-miss at high complexity marks latent ability just below the cut. M-PATH (order of attribute settings) plus M-RTFIRST distinguish a child who derives each attribute deliberately from one who flails; guessing is near-impossible because there is no option set to eliminate, making high-difficulty accuracy unusually clean tail evidence.
age_rationale: Constructing a tile requires holding several partial rule-results in mind and executing multiple coordinated picker taps, which exceeds K-1 working-memory and fine-motor limits; K-1 figural_matrix is served by the selection-based FLU-MATRIX-01. 2-3 constructs on a single attribute (shape) with a 2x2 grid; 4-5 adds color; 6-8 adds count/arithmetic and 3x3 grids with up to three co-acting rules. Large picker buttons and a live preview keep motor demands modest from grade 2 up.

adaptive.content_range: single-attribute 2x2 construction (grades 2-3) up to 3-attribute 3x3 construction with arithmetic/distribution rules (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: number of attributes to construct 1 to 3
rule type constant to progression to distribution-of-three to arithmetic
count range for the numeric attribute
adaptive.notes: Fully procedurally generable from a rule x attribute grammar; the answer key is the attribute vector so per-attribute scoring and parallel clones for consistency checks are automatic; supports a bottomless above-level bank for ceiling probing.

engagement_hook: You are the tile-maker: forging the missing piece attribute-by-attribute and watching the machine light up when your built tile is right feels more agentive than picking from a menu.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Pair color with shape so color-vision differences never decide an item; keep picker buttons large to remove fine-motor load; live preview and undo prevent slip errors; ghost-hand plus warm-up neutralizes construction-novelty variance; cap attribute count for young bands so working memory does not confound rule derivation; do not over-reward speed since deliberate construction is expected.

name: Fix the Glitch
topics_techniques_covered: figural_matrix: a fully-filled matrix contains ONE cell that violates the row/column relational rules; find the broken cell
figural_matrix: Raven-like relational rules running across rows and columns
figural_matrix: RPM rule taxonomy - constant-in-a-row, progression, distribution-of-three, arithmetic add/subtract of a numeric attribute
figural_matrix: logical relations (XOR, OR, AND, consistent union) over attributes (size, color, position, number)
figural_matrix: cognitive-model-driven difficulty (rule count x abstraction x perceptual load)
one_liner: Every cell of a matrix is filled but one is wrong; the child taps the single cell that breaks the pattern.
interaction: A 2x2 or 3x3 matrix is shown completely filled. Exactly one cell violates the rules running across its row and column. The child taps that cell (it lifts and highlights; tapping another moves the choice), then taps GO to confirm. Short quick trials run back-to-back. One decisive tap is the answer; no typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand scans left-to-right along each row with a small nod on cells that fit, then taps firmly on the cell that clashes, which flashes and snaps back into rule. A warm-up 2x2 with three red circles and one blue circle runs unscored first.

learning_science.why: Spotting a violation requires holding the generative rule and comparing every cell to it, a different and often more sensitive probe than completing a single blank.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The whole matrix is shown and the child must locate the inconsistency, forcing full row-and-column rule verification rather than local completion.
learning_science.source: Siegler (2002), in Microdevelopment: Transition Processes in Development and Learning

learning_science.why: The slowest responses across many quick trials index ability better than peak speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The type runs several short violation-spotting trials and logs RT variability and the slowest lapses rather than crediting raw speed.
learning_science.source: Coyle (2003), Intelligence 31(6)

learning_science.principle: Cognitive load theory - minimize extraneous load
learning_science.why: Instructions add extraneous load that masks the reasoning measured.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A wordless ghost-hand scan-and-tap and a single large tap target carry all instruction so working memory is spent on rule-checking.
learning_science.source: Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas (1998), Educational Psychology Review 10(3)

tail_precision_rationale: Running several fast violation-spotting trials yields M-RTVAR and M-LAPSE, whose low variability and few slow lapses track ability better than peak speed (worst-performance rule) and resist coaching. M-ERRTYPE reads which cell a wrong tap chose against a per-rule key, distinguishing a defensible alternative reading (a second cell that is only mildly off) from a random or salience-driven miss, refining placement below the cut. M-RTFIRST captures the reflective scan-before-tap of strong reasoners, and because trials are short and cloneable the type contributes many stable RT samples that firm up the tail estimate without fatigue.
age_rationale: K-1 sees a 2x2 with one obvious single-attribute mismatch and a big tap target, which is immediately intuitive as spot-the-different-one. 2-3 uses a 3x3 with a single-rule violation; 4-5 and 6-8 raise to multi-rule matrices where the broken cell is only detectable by checking a progression or arithmetic relation, with perceptually close cells. Single-tap response and no reading keep the youngest band supported.

adaptive.content_range: 2x2 single-attribute obvious mismatch (K-1) up to 3x3 multi-rule violations where only one relation is broken and cells are perceptually confusable (6-8)
difficulty_levers: number of co-acting rules that must be checked 1 to 3
how subtly the broken cell deviates (adjacent color vs far color, off-by-one count)
rule type constant to progression to arithmetic to logical
adaptive.notes: Generate a rule-consistent matrix then perturb exactly one cell by one attribute keyed to a named rule; unlimited clones, precise difficulty control, and many short trials for stable RT statistics.

engagement_hook: Debugging the machine: hunting the one glitchy cell and watching it snap back into place gives a satisfying detective-fix moment, and quick rounds create a light game rhythm.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Ensure exactly one cell is defensibly wrong (audit that no second cell can be read as the violation) so error coding is meaningful; pair color with shape/pattern; do not reward mere speed; a single large tap target removes motor load; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; keep rule count low for young bands so scanning load does not confound reasoning.

name: Put It In Order
topics_techniques_covered: figure_series: a sequence changes by a consistent rule across the row; reconstruct the ordering rather than pick the next figure
figure_series: row progression on one or more attributes (size up, fixed-step rotation, increasing count)
figure_series: an incomplete progressive sequence with a missing MIDDLE frame to be placed (CFIT-style)
figure_series: simple repeating or growing picture pattern (AB AB, or +1 dot each step)
one_liner: Scrambled figures from a pattern are jumbled; the child puts them back into the right left-to-right order.
interaction: A row of empty slots sits above a tray of shuffled figures (one variant fixes the first and last frame and asks for the middle ones). The child taps a tray figure to drop it into the next empty slot, or taps a placed figure to send it back to the tray; frames snap to slots. When all slots are filled the child taps GO. Large tap targets; no typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand lifts the first frame into slot one, then the next, sweeping left-to-right so the growing progression is visible, then taps GO and the ordered row animates its change. A 3-frame small-to-big warm-up runs unscored first.

learning_science.principle: Fluid intelligence via inductive rule extraction
learning_science.why: Recovering the order requires inferring the progression rule and mapping it onto a spatial sequence, a culture-fair Gf process.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Frames are built from attribute progressions (size, count, rotation) so ordering loads inductive reasoning rather than crystallized knowledge or notation.
learning_science.source: Cattell (1963), Journal of Educational Psychology 54(1)

learning_science.why: Producing a full ordering is a stronger probe of the represented rule than choosing a single continuation, because every adjacency must respect the rule.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child reconstructs the entire sequence (or inserts missing middles) so all pairwise steps, not just the last one, must be correct.
learning_science.source: Lashley (1951), Cerebral Mechanisms in Behavior (The Problem of Serial Order in Behavior)

learning_science.why: A reconstructed order yields per-position graded evidence and blocks lucky single-pick guessing.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scoring is per-slot-correct (polytomous) so a nearly-right ordering (one adjacent swap) earns graded credit.
learning_science.source: Embretson & Reise (2000), Item Response Theory for Psychologists

tail_precision_rationale: Reordering turns one item into per-position evidence: M-POLY grades how many slots are correctly placed so a single adjacent swap is distinguished from a scrambled guess, placing the child precisely where next-term selection cannot. M-PATH records the placement order - strong reasoners often anchor the extreme (smallest/largest) frames first and fill inward - while M-EFF compares moves to the minimal placement count and M-REV counts send-backs, so economical, correctly-ordered solving is a clean tail separator even at equal final accuracy. M-RTFIRST captures rule-extraction latency before the first placement.
age_rationale: Ordering three frames by an obvious single attribute is accessible to K-1 (tap-to-place, no reading, big targets). 2-3 orders four frames on one attribute; 4-5 combines two attributes or inserts missing middles; 6-8 uses fixed-step rotation plus count/size progressions and longer sequences with confusable near-duplicate frames. The reconstruction interaction scales smoothly across all four bands.

adaptive.content_range: order three single-attribute frames (K-1) up to reconstruct or complete a five-frame multi-attribute progression with rotation (6-8)
difficulty_levers: step size and whether the step is constant or accelerating
adaptive.notes: A sequence grammar generates the ordered frames then shuffles them; the ordered key gives automatic per-position scoring and unlimited parallel forms for consistency and drift checks.

engagement_hook: Un-jumbling a scrambled pattern into a satisfying marching order, with the completed row playing its progression as a little animation reward.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Avoid numerals and reading (use dots/shapes for count); large tap-to-place targets remove fine-drag demands; ensure a unique correct ordering (no symmetric ambiguity) so per-position scoring is fair; pair color with shape; keep pacing self-directed so processing speed does not contaminate the reasoning score; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Same-Change Machine
topics_techniques_covered: figure_analogy: A is to B as C is to ? - infer the A-to-B transformation and PERFORM it on C rather than select the result (NNAT format)
figure_analogy: two figures related by a rule then a third figure; produce the figure completing the analogy (ICAR figural analogies)
figure_analogy: simple A:B::C:? with one clear change (e.g. big to small)
figure_analogy: A:B::C:? with two shapes changing by one combined rule (size and shade)
one_liner: A first shape changes into a second; the child makes the SAME change happen to a third shape by applying transform tools.
interaction: The top row shows A with an animated arrow morphing it into B. Below sits C and a palette of transform tiles (shrink/grow, rotate a quarter-turn, flip, recolor, add/remove a dot). Each tap applies that transform live to C; an undo tile steps back. The child performs the same change(s) they saw from A to B, then taps GO. No option tray to pick a finished figure; no typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand replays the A-to-B morph (e.g., big shrinks to small), moves to C, taps the matching transform tile, and C visibly performs the same change; the row lights up. Warm-up: A big circle shrinks to a small circle, so the child taps shrink on a big square.

learning_science.why: Analogical reasoning is mapping the relation, not the surface, from base to target.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child must extract the A-to-B transformation and re-apply it as an action to C, so only relational mapping - not surface matching to a ready option - is credited.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), Cognitive Science 7(2)

learning_science.why: Children move from surface to relational responding as knowledge and working memory grow, setting a floor age for abstract figural analogy.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Bands start at grades 2-3 with a single obvious transform and add a second combined transform by 6-8, matching the relational shift.
learning_science.source: Rattermann & Gentner (1998), in Piaget, Evolution, and Development

learning_science.why: Producing the transformed figure encodes the relation more deeply and prevents recognition-only guessing.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child enacts the transformation to build the answer instead of selecting a finished figure, so the response reflects genuine rule application.
learning_science.source: Slamecka & Graf (1978), Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory 4(6)

tail_precision_rationale: Because the child ENACTS the transformation, M-PATH logs exactly which transforms were applied and in what order, and M-RULEID reports how many of the required transforms were correctly applied - so on a two-transform analogy a child who nails one but not both is graded between full and zero, separating one-rule from two-rule mappers at the tail. M-POLY gives that graded credit; M-ERRTYPE names the failure mode (right transform wrong magnitude, wrong transform, or extra transform applied). M-RTFIRST captures the map-before-act latency typical of strong reasoners and M-REV distinguishes confident enactment from trial-and-error toggling.
age_rationale: Figural analogy requires holding an abstract transformation and re-applying it; reliable mapping over arbitrary transforms is not dependable until roughly grades 2-3 (ages 7-9), so K-1 is excluded to avoid measuring the relational shift rather than reasoning (Goswami 1992; Rattermann & Gentner 1998). 2-3 uses one salient transform; 4-5 a single transform with a distractor tile that over-applies; 6-8 combines two transforms. Large transform tiles and an undo keep motor demands low.

adaptive.content_range: one obvious transform A:B::C:? enacted on C (grades 2-3) up to two combined transforms with tempting near-transform tiles (6-8)
difficulty_levers: number of transforms to apply 1 to 2+
transform type: size, rotation, fill/shade, count, reflection, add/delete element
presence of over-application or wrong-magnitude transform tiles
adaptive.notes: A:B::C:? items generate from a transform grammar; the correct answer is the ordered transform set applied to C so per-transform scoring and clones are automatic; difficulty scales cleanly by transform count.

engagement_hook: A magic-change machine: you learn a spell by watching A become B, then cast the same spell on C with your own hands and watch it transform.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Exclude K-1 to avoid measuring the relational shift instead of reasoning; include over-application and wrong-magnitude transform tiles so surface tapping does not score; pair shade/color with shape; large transform tiles plus undo remove motor and slip load; the ghost-hand morph plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Sort the Families
topics_techniques_covered: figure_classification: partition a set of figures into groups that each share a hidden property (rather than pick one belonger)
figure_classification: figures share a generated attribute value (e.g. same number of sides); group all that fit
figure_classification: group by BOTH generated attributes (shape count AND fill)
odd_one_out: several figures share a generated rule except one; the outlier ends up alone in its own family
nonverbal_deduction: assign figures to a group only if a spatial condition holds (a dot inside the circle but outside the square; star above the box AND inside the ring)
one_liner: A pile of figures belongs to two hidden families; the child taps each figure to send it to the family it belongs in.
interaction: Six to eight figures sit in a pool between two (or three) color-coded family zones shown by icon, not words. Tapping a figure cycles its family tag through the available colors (and back to unassigned); the figure tints to its current family. When every figure is assigned the child taps GO. An outlier that fits no family is left in its own single-member zone. Tap-to-cycle; no drag precision, no typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand picks up the first figure, hovers it over each family zone (weighing it), then taps it into the matching family which glows to accept; it repeats for a second figure of the other family. Warm-up: sort four figures into a red family and a blue family by color.

learning_science.why: Building the categories requires inducing the concept that unifies each family, a core fluid-reasoning process.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child must infer each family's shared property from the members and test every figure against it, mirroring concept attainment across the whole set at once.
learning_science.source: Bruner, Goodnow & Austin (1956), A Study of Thinking

learning_science.why: Family membership can rest on relational or conjunctive properties, not just surface features.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Higher bands require grouping by BOTH attributes or a spatial relation, pushing from surface to relational classification.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), Cognitive Science 7(2)

learning_science.why: Starting concrete then moving abstract supports transfer of the classification schema.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 groups familiar single attributes (color); older bands fade to abstract shape attributes and conjunctions.
learning_science.source: Fyfe, McNeil, Son & Goldstone (2014), Educational Psychology Review 26(1)

tail_precision_rationale: Partitioning a whole set produces per-figure evidence: M-POLY grades how many figures land in the correct family so one item yields many bits and a single misassignment is distinguished from a broken partition. M-PATH shows the assignment order - confident classifiers place the clear exemplars first and reserve the ambiguous or outlier figures for last - while M-EXPLORE and M-REV count re-taps that reveal hypothesis revision versus first-pass certainty. M-ERRTYPE names which attribute a misassigned figure honored (a one-attribute match on a two-attribute family), a graded near-miss that places the child just below the conjunctive-classification cut.
age_rationale: Assigning figures to two color families by tapping is immediately intuitive for K-1 (no reading, large targets, tap-to-cycle needs no drag precision). 2-3 groups by a single abstract attribute; 4-5 adds a third family or an outlier; 6-8 requires conjunctive or spatial-relation membership with confusable figures. The partition interaction and tap-to-cycle tagging support the youngest band while scaling to the tail.

adaptive.content_range: sort into two single-attribute families (K-1) up to three families or conjunctive/spatial-relation membership with an outlier (6-8)
difficulty_levers: single attribute vs conjunction of two vs spatial relation
presence of an outlier that fits no family
adaptive.notes: Family rules and members are procedurally sampled with a uniqueness audit so the intended partition is the only defensible one; the group key gives automatic per-figure scoring and unlimited clones.

engagement_hook: Reuniting scattered figures with their families - each correct placement glows a welcome, and discovering what makes a family is intrinsically satisfying.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Audit that the members determine a unique partition (no figure defensibly fits two families) so per-figure scoring and near-miss coding are valid; pair color with shape/pattern for color-vision differences; keep the youngest categories culturally common; large tap-to-cycle targets remove motor load; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Name the Secret Rule
topics_techniques_covered: visual_rule_discovery: a few input-to-output grid examples demonstrate a transformation rule; identify WHICH rule is operating (rather than construct the output or sort figures)
visual_rule_discovery: one worked example shows a small grid changing (e.g. all shapes shift right); select the rule that produced it
inductive_reasoning: infer the general rule from worked examples and choose the matching rule among candidates
one_liner: After watching a grid change from before to after, the child taps which of several rule-cards shows that same change.
interaction: The top shows one or two worked example pairs (a before grid with an arrow to an after grid) produced by a hidden rule. Below sit 3-4 rule-cards, each illustrating a DIFFERENT candidate rule as its own little before-to-after mini pair. The child taps the rule-card whose change matches the examples (tap another to switch), then taps GO. A lamp can be tapped to reveal one more worked example before committing. Selection by tap; no typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand points along the worked example (before, then after, tracing the movement), then slides to the matching rule-card and taps it; the card glows and the example replays on it. Warm-up: an obvious recolor-everything-blue rule among clearly different cards.

learning_science.principle: Dual search of hypothesis and experiment spaces
learning_science.why: Rule discovery is searching a space of candidate rules and testing them against evidence, the core of inductive/scientific reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Candidate rules are made explicit as cards so the child evaluates competing hypotheses against the worked examples rather than only producing an output.
learning_science.source: Klahr & Dunbar (1988), Cognitive Science 12(1)

learning_science.why: How much evidence a child needs to lock the rule indexes learning efficiency beyond a static score.
learning_science.concrete_decision: An optional extra worked example (a graduated prompt) is available and logged, turning the item into a mini learning-rate probe.
learning_science.source: Grigorenko & Sternberg (1998), Psychological Bulletin 124(1)

learning_science.why: A studied before-to-after example lowers extraneous load and speeds rule abstraction.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The rule is conveyed entirely through worked example pairs (no notation) so the task loads induction, not symbol reading.
learning_science.source: Renkl & Atkinson (2003), Educational Psychologist 38(1)

tail_precision_rationale: M-HINT and the derived M-HYP capture how many worked examples the child needed before committing: locking the correct rule from a single example is a strong dynamic-assessment learning-rate signal with tail validity beyond accuracy. M-ERRTYPE reads which competing rule a wrong pick chose (a partial rule that matches one example but not both), grading how close the child's induced hypothesis was and placing them below the cut. M-PROG tracks any switch of selection as evidence accrues (does the child revise toward the right rule when the extra example appears), and M-RTFIRST indexes hypothesis-search time before the first pick.
age_rationale: Choosing among explicit candidate rules requires generating and comparing hypotheses against evidence, which is unreliable in K-1; the youngest band is served by the concrete FLU types. 2-3 discriminates a single obvious transform from clearly different candidates; 4-5 uses less salient single-feature rules and closer distractor rules; 6-8 uses conjunctive or two-step rules whose distractor cards each match part of the evidence. Tap selection with large cards keeps motor demands modest.

adaptive.content_range: pick an obvious single transform among distinct rule-cards (grades 2-3) up to identify a two-step/conjunctive rule among partially-matching distractor rules (6-8)
difficulty_levers: rule complexity: single feature to conjunction to two-step
how many candidate rules and how partially they match the evidence
number of worked examples shown before hints
adaptive.notes: Rules and grids are program-sampled and distractor rules are chosen to each satisfy part of the evidence, requiring an audit that only the keyed rule fits all examples; high-throughput cloning with a uniqueness check.

engagement_hook: Cracking a secret code: watching a grid transform and then catching the exact rule that did it - with the option to ask for one more clue - delivers a detective aha.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Audit that only the keyed rule fits every worked example so distractor-rule coding is valid; keep the extra-example lamp non-punitive but logged; pair color with shape/pattern; large rule-cards and single-tap selection remove motor load; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; exclude K-1 to avoid floor effects misread as low ability.
